newsitem.title: UK: U.S. seen ready to risk diplomatic damage on Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seen ready to risk diplomatic damage on Iraq.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent

Fresh U.S. attacks on Iraq could cause trouble with Russia, some key NATO allies and much of the Arab world -- but all the signs are that Washington is prepared to get on with the bombing and accept the diplomatic damage.

U.S. warplanes and an aircraft carrier headed to the Gulf on Friday for widely expected attacks to punish Iraqi President Saddam Hussein, after he defied Western patrols of no-fly zones over Iraq and backed a Kurdish group in northern Iraq.
With less than two months to the U.S. presidential election in November, analysts say there is little choice for President Bill Clinton if he is to fend off charges of weakness at home.
Indeed, Clinton is likely to reinforce his lead over Republican challenger Bob Dole if he attacks Iraq.
By using Stealth aircraft, high-altitude bombers and cruise missiles, the risk of casualties to U.S. forces -- which would be very bad news for Clinton -- is minimised.

Moreover, analysts say the increasing tendency of the United States to pursue foreign policy goals unilaterally has proven popular with voters who have little patience with the reservations of allies and partners.
"Looking tough never does a U.S. president any harm," said one European diplomat who asked not to be identified.

"Saddam has called the Americans' bluff and Clinton is boxed in politically on this issue," said Michael Cox, an expert on U.S. foreign policy with the Royal Insitute of International Affairs (RIIA) in London.
"All the signs are that he will take further action."
Last week, U.S. planes and ships launched 44 cruise missiles at southern Iraqi air defences in retaliation for an Iraqi military action against a Kurdish faction in the north.
U.S. Republicans have criticised the missile strike as an inadequate response and many commentators have seen a limited victory for Saddam so far in his showdown with Washington.
The Iraqi leader has wrested back control of northern Iraq for the first time in five years and split Washingon from most of its Gulf War allies. He has been unmoved by U.S. strikes.
All of this is likely to goad Clinton into action, despite a public softening of U.S. rhetoric in the last 24 hours.
"The Americans will send a clear signal this time," said Ailie Saunders of the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).
Nevertheless, the United States knows that it will face trouble abroad -- and criticism at the U.N. General Assembly which opens next week in New York -- if the attacks go ahead.
The allied unity which enabled the United States to forge a coalition after Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990 has now fragmented.
Russia and China have both opposed the U.S. threats of renewed attacks. Moscow said further action would require the approval of the U.N. Security Council.
NATO ally Turkey, which is the base for allied planes patrolling the no-fly zone in northern Iraq, has said it favours a diplomatic approach to the problems with Baghdad.

With the notable exception of Britain, nearly always a loyal U.S. ally, many other NATO members have private doubts about Washington's approach. Although it will help Clinton in his bid for a second term, diplomats say it will do little else other than to boost tensions in the already volatile Gulf region.
France opposed last week's U.S. missile strikes but seems to be preparing the ground for a more qualified approach this time.
French President Jacques Chirac said on Thursday France was "committed to the arrangements put in place after the Gulf War by the allies" to protect minorities like the Kurds in Iraq.

Diplomats said this was a reference to the enforcement of the no-fly zone, in which French, British and U.S. planes take part. Since any more U.S. action would be a retaliation for Iraqi missile attacks on planes enforcing the no-fly zone, France may be prepared to accept that they are justified.
But there are also serious misgivings about the U.S. action in much of the Arab world, at a time when the Middle East peace process is in grave trouble.
Nevertheless, diplomats say the United States has shown an increasing tendency to act unilaterally on foreign policy issues in recent months when it felt the need to do so.

Washington has publicly blocked U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali's bid for a second term and enraged allies by introducing laws that would punish foreign firms for doing business with U.S. enemies like Iran, Libya and Cuba.
